walkthroughs.body_html:
Practical Skills — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Practical Skills brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Practical Skills.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which apparatus most accurately measures 25.0 cm³ for titration?
options: Beaker
Measuring cylinder
Pipette
Conical flask

mcqs.q: The end point of a strong acid-strong base titration is best detected by:
options: Methyl orange or phenolphthalein
Universal indicator
Silver nitrate
Limewater

mcqs.q: Does a catalyst affect the position of equilibrium?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
No — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but at the same position.
A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
A catalyst shifts the equilibrium towards the products.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.
Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
